question_text: A 23-year-old woman presents to the physician with complaints of pain and paresthesias in her left hand, particularly her thumb, index, and middle fingers. She notes that the pain is worse at night, though she still feels significant discomfort during the day. The patient insists that she would like urgent relief of her symptoms, as the pain is keeping her from carrying out her daily activities. On physical examination, pain and paresthesias are elicited when the physician percusses the patient’s wrist as well as when the patient is asked to flex both of her palms at the wrist. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in the management of this patient’s condition?

                    ### Question
                    A 23-year-old woman presents to the physician with complaints of pain and paresthesias in her left hand, particularly her thumb, index, and middle fingers. She notes that the pain is worse at night, though she still feels significant discomfort during the day. The patient insists that she would like urgent relief of her symptoms, as the pain is keeping her from carrying out her daily activities. On physical examination, pain and paresthesias are elicited when the physician percusses the patient’s wrist as well as when the patient is asked to flex both of her palms at the wrist. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in the management of this patient’s condition?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Corticosteroid injection
opb. Electromyography testing
opc. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
opd. Splinting
ope. Surgical decompression

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient's symptoms of pain and paresthesias in the left hand, worsened at night and elicited on wrist percussion and flexion, are indicative of likely median nerve compression at the wrist (carpal tunnel syndrome). The most appropriate initial step in management is splinting to relieve symptoms and provide support. Evidence paths support the use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs in carpal tunnel syndrome, but splinting remains the consensus-aligned first-line approach.
